title: Building Mood State Classifiers to Inform Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of Treatment-Resistant Bipolar Depression
text: Bipolar disorder, an often-debilitating condition associated with a high risk for suicide, is characterized by dramatic and recurrent shifts in mood, energy levels and behavior ranging from the lows of depression (lasting weeks or months) to the highs of mania (lasting at least a week). There is an urgent need for more effective treatments of the depressive phase of bipolar disorder; accordingly, this study will test whether deep brain stimulation (DBS), a neurosurgical procedure widely using in movement disorders, is effective and safe in 10 patients with bipolar depression. To reduce the risk of inducing mania, emerging signs such as decreased need for sleep, increased activity, rapid speech, and elevated mood, will be monitored using a variety of mobile monitoring methods (e.g., wearables, smart phone readouts, audio diaries, etc.) together with recording of brain activity by the DBS device.

title: Project 1: Molecular Predictors of Prostate Cancer Progression and Mortality
text:
The goals of this proposal are to use population methods to recruit a diverse cohort of men with incident prostate
cancer, perform combined evaluation of rare variant germline DNA repair genes (e.g. BRCA2) and a novel multi-
ancestry polygenic risk score, to develop a clinical-grade paired tumor-germline assay and determine the
biological significance of high PRSm and specific PRSm variants using tumor molecular profiles. We will also
conduct a tailored prostate cancer screening clinical trial including at-risk first-degree relatives of men recruited
through population methods and determine patterns of interest, enrollment and adherence to prostate cancer
screening. Overall, we seek to investigate the synergy of germline genetic information with relevance to a diverse
population with the goal of improving risk prediction and tailored PC screening for men across multi-ancestry
populations.

title: High-Resolution Multiplexed MRI at Ultrahigh Field
text:
This R01 project will develop and validate a new MRI technology for multiplexed imaging of multiple molecules
in the proton spin system at ultrahigh field (7T) in high imaging speed and spatial resolution. The technology will
provide an unprecedented capability to acquire a comprehensive set of quantitative molecular, physiological and
structural biomarkers for multifaceted tissue characterization. The technical capability will significantly enhance
our ability to diagnose and characterize diseases and assess their treatment response and efficacy for
personalized and precision medicine.

title: De novo design of pro domains for TGF superfamily folding, expression, and function
text:
De novo design of pro domains for TGF superfamily folding, expression, and function
This proposal seeks to establish a fundamentally new approach to regulate activity of transforming
growth factor beta (TGF-β) superfamily growth factors (GFs) using defined spatiotemporal internal
or external cues. The TGF-β superfamily is a group of cysteine knot growth factors that play
essential roles in central developmental processes and are promising candidates for therapeutic
intervention. This approach is significant and relevant to public health as potential clinical uses of
these growth factors include: wound healing, bone and cartilage regeneration, and cancer.

title: Project 2: Memory-like NK cell therapy for AML relapsed after allogeneic transplant
text:
Our research will test a new cellular immunotherapy, called memory-like natural killer cells, in a clinical trial for
patients with acute myeloid leukemia who have relapsed after allogeneic hematopoietic cell (bone marrow)
transplantation. Additional goals of this research are to identify correlates of leukemia response or resistance to
this new treatment, impact on other components of the immune system, and to test new approaches to optimize
the response and recognition of AML by memory-like NK cells. We also expect that this research will lead to
new combination immunotherapy treatments for patients with leukemia in the future.

title: Copper scavenging mechanisms in fungal pathogens
text:
Every year, millions of humans are exposed to fungi that naturally live in soil or are common in
the environment, leading to disease. In this proposal, we will investigate new pathways by which
soil-dwelling pathogenic fungi have adapted to overcome metal-restrictive growth conditions
reminiscent of those observed in humans during microbial infection. The analogs to the metal-
binding small molecules and proteins studied in this proposal have direct clinical relevance, and
further study into their basic biology and mechanisms will lay the foundation for advancements
in future fungal disease treatment and prevention strategies.

title: CSHL Advanced Techniques in Molecular Neuroscience (2025 - 2029)
text:
CSHL Laboratory Course in Advanced Techniques in Molecular Neuroscience
This application seeks funds to support an advanced neuroscience lab-based short course at
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, New York. The course aims to provide advanced training in state-of-the-art
molecular approaches and concepts in neuroscience. Trainees include advanced graduate students,
postdoctoral researchers and young faculty from throughout the United States and abroad. The selection process
for entry into these courses is highly competitive, and trainees leave the course armed with new techniques,
know-how and potential collaborators to apply to their own areas of research. A significant proportion of trainees
subsequently undertake basic or applied research in diseases of mental health and/or neurological disorders.
Methods and concepts taught in the course are disseminated to the wider research community through the
publication of laboratory manuals and online resources.

title: The role of the ventral tegmental area in motivated behavior
text:
Relevance
Results from the proposed experiments can significantly advance our understanding of neural circuit
mechanisms underlying motivated behaviors. They can shed light on the neural basis of reward and aversion
and thus have major implications for understanding a variety of disorders including schizophrenia, ADHD,
and addiction.

title: Quantitative Imaging Clinical Validation Center at Moffitt Cancer Center
text:
Cancer screening modalities are often associated with false positives, high rates of indeterminate findings,
overdiagnosis, and overtreatment, which are all serious limitations that can be addressed with imaging. Our
group pioneered image biomarker approaches leveraged in the prior funding cycle to create the first and only
EDRN Clinical Validation Center (CVC) to dedicated to the validation of image biomarkers to improve early
detection of cancer. In this renewal application, we build on our initial progress to bring practical automated
solutions to these pressing screening problems.

title: Integrative approaches for predicting protein interactions and applications
text:
The accurate prediction of protein interactions is essential for unraveling the mechanisms underlying numerous
biological processes and for the development of targeted therapeutics. In this proposal, we aim to address the
pressing need for novel computational tools that can predict interactions involving disordered proteins, facilitate in
silico peptide screening, and more. Our goal is to leverage these advancements to identify and explore potential
peptide-based treatments for diabetic wound healing.

title: Generation of DNA memory by bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 systems
text:
Prokaryotic CRISPR-Cas systems enable adaptive immunity against viral infections, and nowadays also provide
eukaryotic gene-editing tools that revolutionized the study and treatment of human diseases. In this proposal,
we aim to uncover the molecule basis for CRISPR-Cas9 antiviral immune memory formation and their evasion
by viruses. This work will substantially advance our understanding of the evolutionary arm race between bacteria
and their phages and help guide the expansion of CRISPR-based technologies to benefit human health.

title: Data Driven Background Estimation in PET
text:
Quantitative PET biomarker imaging promises to play a significant role in delivering precision medicine
for cancer patients, since it can provide accurate biomarker uptake measurements that are necessary for
tumor characterization as well as measuring changes in response to therapy. While PET images
acquired during routine 18F-FDG imaging are highly accurate, it is challenging to maintain the same
performance when imaging large patients (increased multiple scatter, low counts, and reduced tail-fitting
region), in situations where few coincidence events are collected (e.g. imaging at low injected activity
levels for repeat scans or imaging tracers with a low positron yield), or imaging new radiotracers using
isotopes emitting prompt gamma. For PET to fulfill its role in this era, quantification accuracy of PET
images needs to be maintained over a large range of data acquisition protocols, where the quantification
challenge is the accuracy of the scatter and background estimation method that is used to compensate
(correct) for the bias present in the data due to scattered coincidences and prompt gamma events.

title: Striatal Trans-Synaptic Signaling Mechanism in Parkinsonism
text:
Parkinson's disease is a severe neurodegenerative disease. Current treatments are symptomatic and do not prevent disease
progression. Thus, there is a need to identify new therapeutic targets. Neuroplasticity in the striatum has been found to
underlie motor impairments in Parkinson's disease. However, the role of synaptic organizes in these neuroplastic changes
and contribution to motor and non-motor dysfunction is not known. We propose to understand the role of a type of
glutamate receptor which serves as a striatal synaptic organizer in neuroplasticity and behavioral impairment associated
with Parkinson's disease.

title: Conformational mechanisms underlying allosteric regulation of the human serotonin transporter
text:
Dysregulation of the human serotonin transporter (hSERT) contributes to disorders such as anxiety, depression,
and irritable bowel syndrome. Despite intensive study, critical aspects of hSERT regulation—particularly how
endogenous and exogenous allosteric ligands modulate transporter function—remain unclear, limiting our
understanding of their roles in disease. This proposal aims to define the structural and functional basis of
allosteric regulation in hSERT, providing foundational knowledge to support the development of novel therapies
for serotonin-related disorders and to advance our broader understanding of neurotransmitter transporter
biology.

title: Modelling immune and microbiota development to predict health outcomes in children
text:
Environmental exposures during early childhood, including infections and enteric dysfunction, can derail
healthy immune development and lead to increased susceptibility to disease and impaired growth. This
research will leverage existing clinical trials to integrate immune and microbiome profiling in infancy, to identify
early biomarkers that predict key health outcomes, including responses to routine childhood immunisation. By
validating these biomarkers in U.S. children and defining modifiable risk factors, this work will enable
development of targeted interventions to optimize immune development and improve child health outcomes
globally.

title: Well-being in the Face of Adversity: A comparison of the role of positive psychosocial factors on health outcomes in Black women with vs. without Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
text:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and associated health outcomes, particularly cardiovascular
disease (CVD) and renal disease, disproportionately affect Black women, yet the role of positive psychosocial
well-being in this context remains underexplored. Using latent profile analysis to identify distinct psychosocial
well-being profiles, the study aims to explore the impact of these factors on renal and cardiovascular health
outcomes and associated inflammatory markers. This research will also support the career of a junior
investigator dedicated to studying psychosocial factors in chronic disease populations.

title: Understanding the Tropism and Pathogenesis of Pararubulaviruses
text:
This project tackles the challenge of understanding pararubulaviruses (PRubVs), emerging pathogens with
pandemic potential, by delineating their interaction mechanisms with human cells and pathogenic mechanisms
in a small animal model. By leveraging the synergistic expertise of MPIs Drs. Lee and Lim in viral entry,
reverse genetics, organ explant and animal models for viral pathogenesis, it aims to illuminate PRubV
pathogenesis and guide the development of effective countermeasures. This collaborative effort will
substantially advance our preparedness for future zoonotic outbreaks, contributing critically to global health
security.

title: Comparative resistomics of Gram-negative bacterial pathogens
text:
This study will combine experimental evolution with comparative genomics to establish universal and unique
mechanisms driving acquisition of resistance in four difficult-to-treat Gram-negative bacterial pathogens to
four major clinical antibiotics. The developed methodology and obtained results will support rational
optimization of therapeutic regimens and development of new drugs with minimized resistibility.

title: Imaging remyelination in multiple sclerosis using metabolic and ultra-short echo time MRI
text:
This research will develop and validate new metabolic and anatomical magnetic resonance neuroimaging
approaches, which will improve non-invasive monitoring of remyelination processes in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Upon clinical translation, the methods developed in this proposal will serve to ameliorate clinical management of
MS patients, aid develop and validate new therapies promoting remyelination and recovery and, ultimately, lead
to better outcome and patient quality of life.

title: Alternative polyadenylation as a genetic regulatory mechanism to bridge genome to phenome in the nervous system
text:
Anorexia and obesity lie on seemingly opposite ends of the disordered eating spectrum, yet it is well established
that these conditions share appetite circuitry that influence the behavioral decision to eat in excess or scarcity.
Presently, the genetic mechanism that results in this stark phenotypic difference is not known. The goal of this
F99/K00 proposal is to determine if alternative polyadenylation, a rapid activity-dependent RNA processing
mechanism, functionally controls information flow from genome to phenome to meter the development of an
obese phenotype, as this information has the potential to better inform treatments for disordered appetite.
